common_name: Speckled Purple Hull Pea (Old Timer Semi-Crowder Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65F and all frost danger has passed; Speckled Purple Hull, sometimes called Old Timer, is a semi-crowder pea with curved purple pods and cream peas mottled with tan-brown speckles.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Speckled Purple Hull, an old Southern heirloom also known as Old Timer, bears curved, rich purple pods about seven inches long, shelling out to reveal cream-colored peas mottled with distinctive tan-brown speckles, a semi-crowder texture prized for the classic flavor it brings to a pot of Hoppin' John. Its purple pods turn a deeper shade as they mature, making picking time easy to judge, and like other cowpeas it thrives through the hottest, most humid stretch of the Gulf South summer when many other vegetables falter. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage.

common_name: Calhoun Crowder Pea (Wilt- and Nematode-Resistant Louisiana Heirloom Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65F and all frost danger has passed; Calhoun Crowder was developed at the Calhoun Research Station in Louisiana in 1949 and bred for resistance to fusarium wilt and nematodes.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Calhoun Crowder, developed in 1949 at the Calhoun Research Station in Louisiana, bears speckled crowder-type peas packed tightly in the pod, bred specifically for resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematodes, two pressures that limit cowpea production in the heavy, humid soils of the Deep South. Its disease resistance makes it a dependable choice for gardens where cowpeas have struggled in the past, without sacrificing the rich, hearty crowder-pea flavor Southern cooks favor. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage.

common_name: Kentucky Beefsteak Tomato (Golden-Orange Low-Acid Appalachian Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Kentucky Beefsteak is an Appalachian heirloom prized for its golden-orange, notably low-acid flesh and large beefsteak-type fruit.

directions: Start seeds indoors under grow lights 6-8 weeks before the last frost date; transplant outdoors after frost danger has fully passed with a wire cage or stout stake, setting the plant deep to encourage root formation along the buried stem. Kentucky Beefsteak, an heirloom collected from the hills of eastern Kentucky, produces large, meaty, golden-orange fruit with notably low acidity and a mild, sweet flavor, distinguishing it from the more common red and pink Southern beefsteak heirlooms. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and productive through a long summer season in hot, humid Southern conditions. Its low-acid flavor makes it a favorite for slicing and eating fresh for gardeners sensitive to the tang of more acidic tomato varieties.

common_name: Cascade Glaze Collard (Oregon Re-Selection of Heirloom Green Glaze)

planting.note: Direct sow or set transplants 10-12 weeks before the first fall frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cascade Glaze is a modern re-selection of the 1820s Southern heirloom Green Glaze, sharing its glossy, waxy, insect-resistant leaves.

directions: Set transplants or thin direct-sown seedlings to 24-30 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cascade Glaze was bred as a careful re-selection of the classic 1820s Southern heirloom Green Glaze collard, retaining the same smooth, glossy, waxy leaf surface that sheds cabbage worm eggs and deters other leaf-eating pests better than fuzzier-leaved collard varieties, while offering improved uniformity from the breeding work. The open, non-heading rosette produces tender, mild-flavored leaves that hold up well to both heat and light frost, making it productive across a long Gulf South growing season. Harvest outer leaves continuously as the plant grows, and expect sweeter flavor after the first light frosts convert starches to sugars.

common_name: Early Golden Summer Crookneck Squash (Colonial-Era Yellow Crookneck)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Early Golden Summer Crookneck is a colonial-era heirloom squash, first listed commercially in 1828, with warty, curved-neck golden-yellow fruit.

directions: Direct sow in hills in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the danger of frost has passed. Early Golden Summer Crookneck is one of the oldest documented American squash varieties, first offered commercially by Thorburn's seed catalog in 1828 and grown in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden, producing bright golden-yellow, warty-skinned fruit with the classic curved neck of crookneck squash. Its early, prolific bearing and compact bush habit make it a reliable, fast-producing choice for a home vegetable garden. Harvest young, four to six inches long, for the best tenderness and flavor, picking every day or two during peak production to keep the plant setting new fruit.
sources: Monticello Thomas Jefferson Center for Historic Plants
